newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai finance minister quits but impact minor.
newsitem.headline: Thai finance minister quits but impact minor.

text.p: Thai Finance Minister Bodi Chunnananda unexpectedly submitted his resignation on Monday but analysts said the move would have little impact on the markets or the nation's slowing economy.
Bodi said through his ministry's permanent secretary Chatumongkol Sonakul that his resignation sent to Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa would take effect on Tuesday.
"Bodi asked me to announce that today he has submitted his resignation to the prime minister," Chatumongkul told reporters.

Banharn's spokesman, Nikorn Chamnong, told Reuters that the prime minister had not seen Bodi's resignation letter. "If it is true then Chaiyawat Wibulswasdi, deputy finance minister, will be in charge during the caretaker period," he said.
No reasons were given by Bodi for his sudden move but analysts speculated that it must have resulted from a conflict within the government over some key finance ministry matter.

They added that Bodi's resignation would have little impact on markets because he was already a lame-duck official in the outgoing caretaker Banharn cabinet ahead of a general election on November 17.

"This resignation smells of some conflict, but we don't know what. Anyway, it will not make a huge difference because he only had over a month left before elections," said Graham Catterwell, country manager for Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Susheel Narula, head of research at Seamico Securities, said: "It was only a matter of time before a new minister would have come in. This won't have much impact."

There was no immediate reaction in the currency market after news filtered out of Bodi's resignation and dealers said the baht would not be greatly affected because a caretaker minister was not likely to make any major policy changes.

The resignation of Thailand's second finance minister in the 14 months Banharn has been prime minister was, however, seen as a setback for Thailand's image abroad, which has become tainted by a variety of factors.
The economy has slowed, exports are sagging, the stock market is at its lowest level in over three years and Thai banks and finance stocks have been sold heavily by foreign funds.
Moody's Investor Service recently downgraded Thailand's short-term debt rating, making it more expensive for Thai borrowers to take loans from abroad, analysts said.

Unelected Bodi was appointed on May 27 by Banharn to replace sacked finance minister Surakiart Sathirathai. Chaiyawat, who is a deputy central bank governor, was appointed deputy finance minister on September 27.

Chatumongkol, whom Bodi assigned to handle key ministerial duties, said important tasks ahead included a ministry decision on the issue of new banking licences to three consortia that had received preliminary approval for permission to start banks.

A decision on the upgrading of seven foreign bank offshore representative offices to full bank branches was another important matter, he added. But final approval would have to come from a new minister on both the bank issues, he said.
George Morgan, head of the Foreign Brokers Association, said Thailand needed an experienced technocrat or trusted politician to assume Bodi's job.

"You need someone who is going to inspire confidence in the international community. The market would like to see a well-known technocrat with experience of international banking and rating agencies," he said.
"It's now becoming critical if the long-term debt rating is not to be downgraded for a minister to put the right policies in place."
